explanations.positive_explanation: This feature fires on the last token of a self-contained multi-token chunk—whether a foreign phrase (“per se”), an all-caps initialism (“S.D.N.Y.”, “P.I.T.”, “H.O.U.S.E.”), or a multiword proper name (“Brian Head Peak,” “Yolo Bypass,” “St. Julian”)—marking the boundary of that cohesive unit.
explanations.negative_explanation:
Here’s a one‐line abstract summary for each feature’s role:

• Stars: picks up “Stars” used as a proper‐name sports team (e.g. the Texas Stars hockey club).  
• upp: recognizes the subword “Suppose” that opens algebraic word‐problem statements.  
• et: fires on the subword “Let” used to introduce variable definitions in math problems.  
• Jump: marks “Jump To:” style navigation anchors in structured (wiki‐style) pages.  
• Count: identifies “County” as part of a proper name (e.g. the County Records label).  
• Z: flags proper‐name tokens beginning with “Z” (brands, species, personal names).  
• V: flags proper‐name tokens beginning with “V” (brands, products, personal names).  
• MP: spots two‐letter uppercase acronyms (e.g. “MP”) used as section‐heading labels.  
• Export: detects “Export” menu labels for downloading or exporting data/files.  
• Data: detects “Data” as the title word in technical articles on information transmission.  
• Dr: recognizes the “Dr” honorific prefix in academic or professional biography entries.  
• RC: flags “RC” as the Rugby Club abbreviation in sports‐club names.  
• Trigger: catches “Trigger” at the start of film titles (e.g. “Triggermen”).

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron isn’t about “Jason” or “Adam” or any one part of speech at all but about text-structure – it lights up on the very first substantive token after a break (newline, bullet, dash, colon, period, etc). In other words it’s a “clause/sentence-start” or “segment-boundary” detector.
explanations.negative_explanation:
Soft  
Opening word of a quoted song title.

Statistics  
Standalone section heading naming a data or metrics section.

Revolution  
Brand name token at the start of a cosmetic product name.

Is  
The subword or standalone “Is” at the beginning of tokens—marking word-initial “Is-” segments or yes/no questions.

Origin  
Section heading headword “Origin” introducing a “Origin of …” description.

ec  
Root label of a website domain name (e.g. “ecoi.net”).

Tools  
Section heading introducing a list of tools and resources.

Card  
Token sequence “Card” denoting the place name Cardiff in directory or store listings.

Dr  
Honorific prefix “Dr” marking an academic or medical professional’s name.

Effect  
Leading word “Effect(iveness) of …” in scientific article or study titles.

Module  
Product name “ModuleWorks” in software release announcements.

module  
Code keyword “module” in configuration or programming contexts.

INTRODUCTION  
Uppercase section title “INTRODUCTION” in technical or scientific documents.

V  
Initial capital “V” in section headings or titles (e.g. Voting, Videos).

Mark  
Given name “Mark” at the start of a person’s full name.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron is essentially a “clause-pivot” detector: it lights up on the single token that carries the core relation or focus of a sentence or expression—e.g. the main verb in a declarative (“interviews”), the auxiliary in an inverted question (“does/doesn’t”), the conditional or explanatory markers (“?,” “in case,” “i.e.”), or the central technical term in a query (“HTTP,” “git”). It flags the structural head around which the rest of the clause is built.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron fires on the very first word of a new heading or block—be it an article title (“Why,” “What,” “Myth,” “Just,” “Read,” “Dr …”), a code import statement (“import”), or any similar leading token—signaling the start of a distinct section.

explanations.positive_explanation:
Here’s a concise interpretation of what each feature appears to be picking up:

• et (1.000)  
  Marks the “-et” in the tokenization of “Let …,” i.e. the phrasing used to introduce a definition in symbolic math problems.  

• v (0.999)  
  Fires on the single‐letter variable v when authors write “Let v = …” or ask “What is v(…)?” in algebraic contexts.  

• f (0.998)  
  Analogously, picks out the variable or function symbol f in “Let f …” and related function-evaluation questions.  

• 1 (0.998)  
  Responds to the numeral “1” used as a standalone coefficient or constant in algebraic and calculus expressions.  

• te (0.998)  
  Captures the “-te” in instruction verbs such as “Calculate,” “Complete,” “Differentiate,” etc., i.e. the imperatives that kick off problem statements.  

• ig (0.997)  
  Hits on the “-ig” in “digit,” namely in questions like “What is the units digit …?”  

• Development (0.997)  
  Occurs in formal titles or section headings (e.g. “Development of an Instrument …”) in academic write-ups.  

• at (0.997)  
  Marks the final “-at” of the question word “What,” consistently occurring at the start of “What is …?” style queries.  

• units (0.997)  
  Picks up the word “units” in the common phrase “units digit,” i.e. modular-arithmetic questions.  

• e (0.996)  
  Marks the lowercase variable e when it’s introduced (“Let e = …”) in linear-equation solving contexts.  

• try (0.996)  
  Fires on the verb “try” in user-support or troubleshooting posts (“I’m going to try again…”, “Any suggestions?”).  

• upp (0.996)  
  Captures the “upp” of “Suppose,” i.e. the token that begins hypothesis statements in math problems.  

• der (0.996)  
  Hits the “der” in “derivative,” marking calculus questions about first, second, or higher derivatives.  

• E (0.996)  
  Marks uppercase E at the start of proper names or brand names (“Eero,” “Ena,” “eBay”), i.e. named entities beginning with E.
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature detects the little “of/­from/→” link that ties one noun to another—i.e. the genitive or attributive connector (English “of”/participial “connecting,” German von/die, Italian di, Spanish de, Chinese/Japanese 的, etc.).

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron is essentially a “segment‐start” detector: it spikes on tokens that begin new chunks—whether that’s a word or subword (e.g. single letters like “a,” “e,” “y,” prefixes like “NI,” suffixes like “es,” “ow,” numbers like “28,” function words like “an,” “be,” proper-name fragments like “index,” or punctuation‐only chunks like “...” or “[…]”). In short, it marks the onset of a fresh text segment.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron fires on words that serve as section or document headings—the first token of titles, section headers or headlines (in papers, wikis, blogs, news, code logs, etc.), signaling a structural boundary.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron flags standalone, title‐style tokens—often capitalized or all‐caps words and acronyms—that appear at the very start of a document or section header (i.e. headings, titles, labels).
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron fires on the “of Y” head noun in multiword noun phrases—e.g. mine in “friend of mine,” State in “Secretary of State,” Technology in “Institute of Technology,” Mind in “peace of mind,” Interest in “Conflict of Interest,” etc. It marks the complement noun following “of” in fixed expressions and proper names.

explanations.positive_explanation:
Here’s a compact summary of what each feature is detecting:

• coat  
  – Product or brand names that pair a noun with a numeric version (e.g. “Coatforce 10”).  

• Cap  
  – The term “capillary electrophoresis,” i.e. that specific scientific technique.  

• α  
  – Greek-letter prefixes in enzyme/protein names (e.g. “α-amylase”).  

• Touch  
  – Brand, service or product names beginning with “Touch” (e.g. “Touch of Class,” “Touch Tiles”).  

• \(0.998)  
  – LaTeX- or code-style markup commands and environments (e.g. “\section{…},” “\itemize,” “\ccode{…}”).  

• Cash  
  – Business/ad headlines starting “Cash For…” (e.g. “Cash for Trucks”).  

• t  
  – The initial sub-token of “toy” in a toy-product listing (“toy soldier …”).  

• Go  
  – Proper-noun project or building names in title case (e.g. “Gozu House”).  

• DE  
  – All-uppercase artist or band names (e.g. “DEENZI”).  

• Level  
  – Headlines or titles beginning with “Level(s)” (in both scientific papers and product reviews).  

• Hum  
  – Airline names containing “Hummingbird Air.”  

• Drop  
  – Software or app names prefixed by “Drop” (e.g. “Dropbox Carousel,” “Dropwizard Metrics”).  

• Chance  
  – Influencer/streamer handles or real-name mentions in entertainment contexts (e.g. “Chance Sodapoppin”).  

• Switch  
  – Band names ending with “foot” (e.g. “Switchfoot”).  

• Effects  
  – Academic paper titles beginning with “Effects of….”  

• Nit  
  – Biochemical signalling molecule names starting with “Nitric” (e.g. “Nitric oxide”).
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature is picking out code “names” – the identifiers that define or invoke API entities (function- and method-names, class/variable/constants in CamelCase or ALL_CAPS and the `def` keyword that introduces them).

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron is a “header-start” detector: it fires on the very first subword of the first token in titles, section headings or salutations (paper titles, news headlines, letter greetings, etc.), flagging the start of a new document-style segment.
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature fires on numbered “call-outs” and section labels in patent-style texts—i.e. figure references (FIG. 1, FIG. 12, etc.), component or element numerals (101, 102, 110A, etc.), patent/publication numbers, and numbered section headings.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron fires on the very first word of a document or section title (headings, subheadings, paper‐metadata lines, blog “Tag:” labels, patent “Field of the Invention,” etc.), effectively marking the start of a new section or heading.
explanations.negative_explanation: The common thread is that this neuron fires whenever the model is reading an element of a little “kit” or list of things—especially the non-first entries in comma- or hyphen-separated series (e.g. the second half of a short-/long-term pair, the penultimate item before “and,” an entry in a parenthetical enumeration, etc.).

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron flags the very first token of a new heading or title line—i.e. section headers, article titles or bylines, date stamps and similar metadata (e.g. “News,” “Report,” “Sunday,” “Jan.,” “Notes,” etc.).
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron fires on tokens that serve as high-level headings or titles—things like article headlines, archive labels (“Monthly Archives,” “Tag Archives”), Q/A markers (“Q:”, “A:”), section headings and other title-style words at the start of blocks rather than ordinary running text.

explanations.positive_explanation:
• Ball: detects mentions of “balloons” as novelty decorative items.  
• Weight: signals “weight loss” in clinical‐trial contexts.  
• Trend: marks “trends” in epidemiological incidence data over time.  
• Season: flags “seasonal variations” in biological cycles or measurements.  
• ime: recognizes the subword “ime” in words like “prime” or “time,” especially in math/factoring problems.  
• Total: identifies “Total Synthesis” in chemical‐research titles.  
• Effects: highlights study headings beginning with “Effects of …” in experimental biology.  
• Compar: picks out “Comparison of …” in medical outcome or procedural studies.  
• Is: fires on “Isolated …” in descriptions of metabolic or cellular assays.  
• Wire: activates on “Wireless communication systems” in tech/engineering overviews.  
• Report: signals news‐style headlines starting with “Report: ….”  
• Changes: detects “Changes in …” in cellular or physiological research reports.  
• Hard: flags “Hard economic times” in economic or news commentary.  
• IN: marks “INTRODUCTION” section headers in scientific or technical documents.  
• Word: spots “Word of the Year” article or feature headings.  
• CE: recognizes the “CEVO Gfinity” eSports tournament branding.  
• TV: detects the band name “TV on the Radio” and related music‐project news.  
• Part: fires on “Particle agglomeration” in materials‐science contexts.  
• Tax: highlights “Tax Day protests” and tax‐related news events.  
• Universal: marks “Universal Studios” in branded product announcements.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron is a detector for the clitic ­re in English contractions (e.g. you’re, we’re, they’re—and by extension similar tokens like “that’s”), flagging the contracted auxiliary “are” form.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron is a “heading-start” detector: it lights up on capitalized, prominent tokens that kick off titles or section headings (e.g. “Comparative/Comparison…,” “Statistics:,” “Networks…,” “Effects…,” “Edit:,” “Shop by Brand,” “Word of the Year,” “Is working…,” “VPN…,” etc.).

explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron fires on the little “markup” punctuation that denotes code/math formatting—things like back-ticks and fences, dollar‐signs in LaTeX, double-asterisks for bold, leading “#” headings, “//” or “/*” comments, etc. It’s essentially a detector for the delimiters that mark off technical (code or math) spans in markdown/StackExchange‐style text.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron appears to be a “self­-contained subword” detector – it fires most strongly on BPE tokens that by themselves form a complete morpheme or root (often at a word boundary), for example book, type, crop, lack, ruck, ate, iss, etc. In effect it flags those short, standalone chunks that carry the core meaning of a word.
explanations.negative_explanation:
Here’s a single, concise abstract for what each feature is picking up:

• Cap  
  Marks the technical term “capillary electrophoresis” (and its variants) in scientific paper titles, flagging a specialized analytical-chemistry method.

• Trend  
  Flags epidemiological study headings beginning “Trends in …,” e.g. cancer-incidence time-series reports.

• Compar  
  Highlights comparative-study titles that begin “Comparison of …,” indicating side-by-side methodological evaluations.

• Hum  
  Activates on descriptive blog or popular-science passages about hummingbirds, especially flight behavior anecdotes.

• Go  
  Picks up personal-statement headings “Goals and aspirations,” as in essay or statement-of-purpose fragments.

• Development  
  Identifies methodological sections titled “Development and validation …,” often for equations or novel synthetic protocols.

• Is  
  Fires on titles or questions that start with “Is …,” whether clinical case reports (“Isolated tuberculous hepatic abscess…”) or how-to Q&A blog titles (“Is internet marketing …?”).

• Season  
  Marks content about seasons—either sports-season practice write-ups (“Season starts …”) or biological seasonal cycles (“Seasonal variations in …”).

• Out  
  Flags clinical or research headings beginning “Outcome of …,” denoting result-reporting sections.

• Dist  
  Highlights study headings “Distribution of …,” describing geographic or anatomical dispersal patterns.

• End  
  Picks up “Endogenous …” in biomedical contexts, signaling investigations of internally produced biochemical agents.

• Edit  
  Activates on revision notes labeled “Edit: …,” i.e. changelog or update annotations in blogs/articles.

• Effect  
  Marks experimental titles “Effect of …,” denoting investigations of how one variable influences another.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron is essentially a “heading‐detector.” it spikes on the tokens that kick off a new post or section (titles, dates, domain names, acronyms, section‐anchor labels, etc.), as well as on the little uppercase or shorthand bits (UK, JS, .NET, ID, “’re,” “that’s,” “do”) that typically live in headers, titles, or other document metadata.
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature detects “title” tokens—the first word of a headline or section header (whether a news dateline or article title, a press-release heading, a code declaration like class/module, a markdown “#” heading, CLI prompt, log banner, etc.). It flags tokens that open a new top-level section or document.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron fires on the subordinating complementizer/relative‐pronoun “that” (the marker introducing embedded or relative clauses).
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron fires on the very first token of a formatted heading or title (e.g. the opening word of a question‐style or section headline).

explanations.positive_explanation: This channel is a “section-heading opener” detector: it fires on the very first token of formal document titles or headers (e.g. “High” in a paper title, “1.” at the top of a patent section, single letters like “N” or “V” that kick off an acronym or code in a heading).
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron is essentially a “word-end” detector: it lights up on BPE pieces that finish an English word—especially common suffixes (-ed, ‑er, ‑ly, ‑ty, plural ‑s) or standalone word tokens (I, we, she, systems, 2011, etc.). It flags the closing subword of a lexical item.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature detects sentence- or title-initial words—the standalone, capitalized tokens that kick off paper titles, section headings, news headlines, etc.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron lights up on the trailing “-s” (or “As”) that pluralizes all-caps abbreviations—e.g. BCAA→BCAAs, VFA→VFAs, PHA→PHAs, GLP-1RA→GLP-1RAs, etc. It’s essentially a plural-suffix detector for technical acronyms.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature detects code‐comment delimiters and stylized comment markers (e.g. “//**”, “--**”, “/*…*/”, “<!--…-->”) across different programming languages.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron flags the very first, title-case word of a header or title—whether it’s a paper title, article headline, product name, or section heading.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature fires on tokens that serve as high‐level document or section titles/headings—e.g. the words that launch new parts of a technical or scientific text (paper titles, section names like “Introduction,” “Data,” release or module headings, reference lines, etc.). It marks the structural labels that introduce and organize content.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron lights up on the preposition “of” in its partitive/genitive use (e.g. “one of these,” “list of delimiters,” “percent of Americans,” “series of five,” etc.), marking “X of Y” or membership/possession relationships in enumerations and technical descriptions.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron is a general “name/identifier detector.”  It lights up on tokens that label or name things—HTML/XML tag‐opens and attribute names, CSS class/id selectors, file or folder names in paths, function/class/variable identifiers in code, and even proper nouns in running text.
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature flags the leading word of a new section or heading—i.e. the first token of titles, captions or section-opening lines that mark a topic or structural break in the text.
